pos: adv. (in a manner free from just reproach; without just occasion for censure)
etymology: From un-, not, + blame, through Old French blasmer from Greek blasphemein, to speak evil of, + the adverbial -ly. To behave unblameably is to conduct oneself so that no true charge of wrong can be laid.
biblical_def:
Ye are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly and unblameably we behaved ourselves among you that believe.

Paul writes this to the Thessalonians as a plain appeal to the facts of his own conduct among them, calling both the church and God Himself as witnesses. The word stands at the end of a three-part description of apostolic life — holily toward God, justly toward men, unblameably in the sight of all — and it is the capstone because it answers a question observers ask before they ever weigh doctrine: did the preacher's life match his message? Paul's ministry was constantly attacked by those who wished to discredit his gospel by discrediting his character, so he does not merely assert innocence; he appeals to a congregation that watched him daily, labored beside him, and can testify from direct observation. Unblameably does not mean sinless in an absolute sense — Paul elsewhere confesses himself the least of the apostles and a sinner saved by grace — it means nothing in his visible conduct among them gave any honest occasion for reproach. The standard the word sets is a high one for every minister and every believer: a life so transparently consistent with profession that even unfriendly eyes, examining it closely, find no true accusation to bring.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BLAMELESS: without crime, fault, or defect; innocent; guiltless; that cannot justly be charged with wrong.
webster_full: BLAMELESS, a. Without crime or fault; innocent; guiltless; not meriting censure.
UNBLAMEABLY, adv. In a manner free from blame or just censure.
1 Thessalonians 2:10 pairs the word with holily and justly as the believer's threefold answer to God, to men, and to onlookers.
Describes conduct that withstands scrutiny from those most inclined to find fault.
Distinguished from sinlessness; it is a visible consistency, not a claim of inward perfection.
scriptures: Ye are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly and unblameably we behaved ourselves among you that believe:
corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches to the word itself; the recoverable principle is that Christian character must be able to withstand the scrutiny of hostile witnesses, not merely the private judgment of friends.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Unblameably has simply fallen out of common speech rather than being corrupted by it.

The temptation it answers is still very much alive: measuring ministerial integrity by what a sympathetic inner circle will excuse rather than by what an unsympathetic public can observe and still find nothing to charge. Paul's appeal works only because he lived openly before people who had every incentive to expose him if he had given them cause. A church culture that shields leaders from scrutiny, rather than inviting the kind of observation Paul welcomed, trades the apostolic standard for a lesser and more fragile one.

pos: adj. (not liable to just rebuke; beyond reasonable reproach)
etymology: From un-, not, + rebuke, from Old French rebuchier, to repel or check, + -able. That which is unrebukeable gives no ground on which a rebuke could justly land.
biblical_def:
That thou keep this commandment without spot, unrebukeable, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Paul charges Timothy, in the solemn presence of God and of Christ Jesus, to keep the ministerial commission entrusted to him “without spot, unrebukeable” until the Lord's return. The word belongs to the same family as blameless and unreproveable, but it carries a slightly sharper edge: it anticipates an accuser standing ready to rebuke and finds no opening. This is covenantal language appropriate to a charge given before witnesses — Paul has just invoked Pontius Pilate's good confession before Christ as the pattern, and now calls Timothy to a comparable steadfastness that endures to the end, not merely for a season. Unrebukeable does not mean immune from criticism in a worldly sense; Timothy would certainly face hostile voices. It means that whatever charge might be brought against his keeping of the gospel commission would not be a just one. The verse sets the horizon at the appearing of Christ, making plain that the standard is not a performance for the present generation's approval but a charge to be kept intact until the Judge Himself returns to evaluate it.

webster_full: REBUKE, v.t. To check; to reprehend; to reprove sharply.
UNREBUKEABLE, a. Not liable to just rebuke; beyond reasonable reproach.
1 Timothy 6:14 charges Timothy to keep his ministerial commission unrebukeable until Christ's appearing.
Follows Paul's invocation of Christ's good confession before Pontius Pilate as the pattern of steadfastness.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has become archaic rather than corrupted.

The temptation it answers remains current: a minister can be rebuke-proof toward a present congregation's standards and still fail the standard Paul actually names, which is accountability to Christ at His appearing. Trading that eschatological horizon for the narrower goal of avoiding present-day criticism is a quiet but real departure from the charge Paul gave Timothy.

pos: adj. (not open to just reproof; standing without accusation)
etymology: From un-, not, + reprove, from Latin reprobare, to disapprove, + -able. Unreproveable describes a standing against which no charge of disapproval can be justly brought.
biblical_def:
In the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and unblameable and unreproveable in his sight.

Paul writes to the Colossians of the reconciling work accomplished in Christ's body through His death, and the purpose clause that follows is breathtaking: to present them holy, unblameable, and unreproveable in God's own sight. This is not a description of present experience but of a position secured by the cross, to be fully manifested at last. The threefold stacking — holy, unblameable, unreproveable — piles up near-synonyms the way Scripture often does when it wants to leave no crack for doubt: whatever angle an accuser might take, the reconciled sinner stands clear of it in Christ. Unreproveable here is forensic and positional before it is experiential; it describes the standing Christ's finished work secures for those united to Him by faith, not a sinless moral record achieved by the believer's own effort. The verse therefore belongs with justification and reconciliation rather than with sanctification alone, though the hope of standing unreproveable in God's sight is also meant to shape present conduct now.

webster_full: REPROVE, v.t. To chide; to reprehend; to convince of a fault, and represent it to the offender.
UNREPROVEABLE, a. Not open to just reproof; standing clear of accusation.

pos: adv. (in a manner marked by moral excellence; with the strength of character Scripture commends in a woman of worth)
etymology: From virtue, Latin virtus, moral strength or worth, originally bound up with vir, a man, broadened to name moral excellence generally, + the adverbial -ly.
biblical_def:
Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all.

This is the closing verdict of the acrostic poem on the woman who feareth the LORD in Proverbs 31, spoken by her husband and children in the gate where public reputation is weighed. Virtuously here is not decorative praise but a summary of the whole preceding portrait — she rises before dawn, works with willing hands, considers a field and buys it, stretches out her hand to the needy, clothes her household in scarlet, and opens her mouth with wisdom. Her excellence is not passive ornamentation but vigorous, skillful, God-fearing labor exercised within her household under her husband's headship, and it is precisely this combination — strength, industry, wisdom, and the fear of the LORD — that the text calls virtue in a woman. The comparison many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all does not diminish other virtuous women; it crowns this one as the model toward which the praise of all others points. The chapter closes where it should: her own works praise her in the gates, a public honor earned by private faithfulness, not claimed by self-promotion.

webster_full: VIRTUE, n. Moral goodness; the practice of moral duties, and the abstaining from vice.
VIRTUOUSLY, adv. In a manner marked by moral excellence and strength of character.
Proverbs 31:29 crowns the woman who feareth the LORD as the one who excels all who have done virtuously.
Her virtue is industrious and wise, not merely decorative or passive.

corruption_summary: Modern secular feminism redefines a woman's worth by autonomous self-actualization and career achievement detached from the home, household, and the fear of the LORD that Proverbs 31 actually commends.
corruption_paragraphs: Second-wave and later feminist thought recast female excellence as self-defined achievement outside the household, often treating domestic industry as confinement rather than, as Proverbs 31 presents it, a field of vigorous strength, skill, and wisdom exercised under God.

Scripture's portrait does not oppose capability to domesticity; the virtuous woman buys fields, trades profitably, and clothes her household in fine linen, all while her heart's center is the fear of the LORD and her household's good, not autonomous self-definition apart from it. Recovering virtuously means recovering both halves at once: real strength and skill, ordered toward God and household rather than against them.

pos: adv. (knowingly; with full awareness and intention)
etymology: From Old English witan, to know, the same root that gives wit and wisdom, + the adverbial -ly. To do a thing wittingly is to do it with full knowledge of what one is doing.
biblical_def:
And Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it upon Ephraim's head, who was the younger, and his left hand upon Manasseh's head, guiding his hands wittingly; for Manasseh was the firstborn.

The aged, nearly blind Jacob (called Israel) is blessing Joseph's two sons, and the text takes pains to specify that his crossed hands were not the fumbling of failing eyes but a deliberate, knowing act. Manasseh was the firstborn and would have expected the right hand of greater blessing; Jacob instead wittingly places his right hand on Ephraim, the younger, reversing the expected order. This single adverb carries real theological weight: it rules out the possibility that the blessing's reversal was an old man's mistake, and insists instead that it was prophetic intention, consistent with the pattern already running through Genesis in which the LORD's sovereign election repeatedly passes over the firstborn by human expectation — Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, and now Ephraim over Manasseh. Wittingly thus guards the doctrine of divine election from the charge of accident. What looks to the eye like confusion in a dying patriarch's hands is, the text insists, the deliberate unfolding of God's own sovereign choice, exercised through Jacob's clear-sighted faith rather than his failing sight.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from WIT: knowledge, understanding; wittingly: knowingly; with knowledge; not ignorantly or by chance.
webster_full: WIT, n. Knowledge; understanding; the faculty of knowing.
WITTINGLY, adv. Knowingly; with knowledge or design; not ignorantly or by mistake.
Genesis 48:14 specifies that Jacob's crossed hands on Ephraim and Manasseh were deliberate, not an old man's error.
Guards the pattern of divine election from being read as accident.

What the verse guards against is a live temptation nonetheless: reading surprising providences, especially ones that overturn expected hierarchies of birth order, merit, or status, as mere accidents of circumstance rather than as the deliberate outworking of God's sovereign election. Jacob's hands moved wittingly; so does the LORD's hand in every life He orders.

pos: adj. (possessing keen, skillful understanding; ingenious; in Proverbs, marked by shrewd and fruitful discernment)
etymology: From Old English witan, to know, the same root behind wit and wittingly; witty originally named keenness of understanding before it narrowed in modern speech to verbal cleverness alone.
biblical_def:
I wisdom dwell with prudence, and find out knowledge of witty inventions.

Personified Wisdom speaks in Proverbs 8, claiming to dwell together with prudence and to discover knowledge of witty inventions. In the Authorized Version's older sense, witty does not mean amusing or clever in the modern diminished sense of a quip; it means keen, skillful, and ingeniously resourceful — the kind of understanding that finds out solutions, devises, and discerns rightly. Wisdom's inventions here are not entertainments but the fruit of prudent, penetrating discernment applied to real problems and real life, the same wisdom by which, a few verses later, kings reign and princes decree justice. The verse matters doctrinally because it roots all true ingenuity and discovery, whatever field it touches, in wisdom that dwells with prudence rather than apart from it; cleverness divorced from prudence is not what Proverbs 8 calls witty at all, however impressive it may appear. The chapter goes on to identify this wisdom as present with God before the foundation of the world, which the church has long read as pointing forward to Christ, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

Scripture's ideal is cleverness married to discernment and the fear of the LORD, producing invention that serves wisdom's purposes rather than merely amusing an audience.

pos: adv. (of one's own free will; without compulsion)
etymology: From Latin voluntas, will, from velle, to wish or will, + the adverbial -ly. That which is done voluntarily proceeds from the agent's own will rather than external compulsion.
biblical_def:
Now when the prince shall prepare a voluntary burnt offering or peace offerings voluntarily unto the LORD, one shall then open him the gate that looketh toward the east.

Ezekiel's vision of the restored temple sets out ordinances for the prince's regular and occasional offerings, and this verse singles out the case of a freewill offering brought voluntarily, beyond what was commanded for the fixed feasts. The Mosaic law already made room for such offerings (Leviticus 7:16, 22:18-23) as gifts proceeding purely from the worshiper's own devotion rather than from obligation, and Ezekiel's temple vision preserves that category even in its highly ordered, regulated worship. The specific gate-protocol attached to it matters: a voluntary offering still moves through the LORD's appointed order rather than bypassing it. This guards against two opposite errors at once — worship reduced to mere bare obligation with no room for glad, uncompelled devotion, and worship so individualized that it answers to no order at all. Scripture's pattern is freewill devotion exercised within, not apart from, the structure the LORD Himself has appointed for approaching Him.

webster_full: VOLUNTARY, a. Proceeding from the will; acting by choice, not by force or compulsion.
VOLUNTARILY, adv. Of one's own free will; freely; without external constraint.

pos: adv. (not on equal terms; in a manner mismatched in kind or allegiance)
etymology: From un-, not, + equal, from Latin aequalis, even or alike, + the adverbial -ly. To be joined unequally is to be bound to a partner fundamentally mismatched in kind.
biblical_def:
Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?

Paul's image draws on the Mosaic law's prohibition of plowing with an ox and an ass together (Deuteronomy 22:10), two creatures of such different strength and nature that yoking them harms both. Applied to the Corinthian church, the command addresses deep, binding partnership between believer and unbeliever — most directly a warning against compromising alliances and, by long application, against marriage to an unbeliever — grounded not in social snobbery but in the stark incompatibility Paul names in the rhetorical questions that follow: righteousness has no fellowship with unrighteousness, light no communion with darkness, Christ no concord with Belial. The command is not a counsel of isolation from unbelievers generally, since Paul elsewhere assumes ordinary dealings with the world, but a guard against binding, defining partnerships that require shared ultimate allegiance where none exists. Unequally names the mismatch precisely: not a difference of degree, as between two believers of unequal maturity, but a difference of kind, light bound to darkness, that no partnership can genuinely reconcile.

webster_full: UNEQUAL, a. Not equal; not of the same size, number, quality, or degree.
UNEQUALLY, adv. In a manner not matched; disproportionately; of different kind or allegiance.
2 Corinthians 6:14 forbids being unequally yoked, drawing on the ox-and-ass prohibition of Deuteronomy 22:10.

Paul's rhetorical questions — what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? what communion hath light with darkness? — are not rhetorical flourishes but a flat denial that such partnerships can be genuinely reconciled, however winsome the pairing appears. The church recovers the force of unequally by naming plainly where believer and unbeliever, or sound doctrine and compromised doctrine, cannot be yoked without one side being pulled off course.

pos: adj. (excessively or irrationally devoted to religious observance, as charged by an unbelieving or dismissive observer)
etymology: From Latin superstitio, excessive fear of the gods or irrational religious belief, from superstare, to stand over or survive; the term has long been a weapon used by skeptics against sincere religious devotion of any kind.
biblical_def:
Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious.

Paul opens his sermon at the Areopagus with an observation about Athenian religiosity that is double-edged: the word translated superstitious can describe either commendable reverence or excessive, misdirected religious devotion, and Paul's own sermon makes clear he means the latter — a city so crowded with idols that it had erected an altar to an unknown god, covering every religious base without actually knowing the true God behind any of them. Paul does not mock religious seriousness itself; he redirects it, declaring unto them the God whom they ignorantly worship, the Creator who made the world and all things therein, who now commands all men everywhere to repent in light of the resurrection and coming judgment. The Athenians prided themselves on philosophical sophistication while Paul's own gospel would later be dismissed by exactly that sophistication as foolishness. The scene stands as a permanent pattern: cultured unbelief frequently charges biblical religion with the irrationality it cannot see in its own idols, intellectual or otherwise, and the only answer is Paul's own — proclaim the true God plainly rather than conceding the charge.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SUPERSTITION: excessive reverence, or false, unfounded religious fear and observance; superstitious: addicted to or marked by such excess.
webster_full: SUPERSTITION, n. Excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; extreme and unfounded religious fear.
SUPERSTITIOUS, a. Addicted to superstition; full of idle fancies in religion.
Acts 17:22 records Paul's double-edged opening charge against Athenian religiosity before the Areopagus.

corruption_summary: Modern scientific materialism and New Atheism apply superstitious indiscriminately to all revealed religion, including biblical faith in the true and living God, collapsing Paul's distinction between idolatrous devotion and genuine knowledge of the Creator.
corruption_paragraphs: Writers in the New Atheist tradition, and the broader scientism of much secular academia, use superstitious as a catch-all dismissal of any claim to divine revelation, treating biblical faith as indistinguishable from the Athenian altars Paul actually confronted.

Paul's own sermon refuses that collapse: Athens was superstitious precisely because it worshiped an unknown god, many gods covering every contingency without true knowledge of any; the gospel is the opposite move, declaring the one true God who made the world, commands repentance, and has fixed a day of judgment by a risen Christ. Biblical faith is not superstition answered by enlightenment; it is the true knowledge Athens's superstition was groping after without finding.

pos: adv. (in a manner deserving honor; suitably to one's character or calling)
etymology: From Old English weorthig, worthy, of value or honor, + the adverbial -ly. To do worthily is to act in a manner that fits and earns the honor one is given.
biblical_def:
And all the people that were in the gate, and the elders, said, We are witnesses. The LORD make the woman that is come into thine house like Rachel and like Leah, which two did build the house of Israel: and do thou worthily in Ephratah, and be famous in Bethlehem.

The elders and people of Bethlehem bless Boaz at the moment he takes Ruth, the Moabite widow, as his wife, after the legal redemption of Elimelech's inheritance has been settled at the gate. Their blessing reaches back to Rachel and Leah, the matriarchs who built the house of Israel, and forward in a prayer that Boaz himself would do worthily in Ephratah — that his own life and household would prove worthy of the honor just conferred on him as kinsman-redeemer. The blessing is remarkable for how ordinary it sounds and how extraordinary its outcome proves: this marriage, witnessed by the gate's common assembly, becomes the direct line to Obed, Jesse, David, and ultimately Christ. Worthily names the hoped-for correspondence between a man's public honor and his private conduct, a theme the book of Ruth has already made central through Boaz's own worthy, redemptive kindness toward Ruth and Naomi. The gate's blessing asks only that his future match what his past conduct has already shown him to be.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from WORTHY: deserving, suitable, or becoming; worthily: in a manner deserving honor or esteem.
webster_full: WORTHY, a. Deserving; such as merits, suitable to the character or station.
WORTHILY, adv. In a manner deserving honor; suitably to one's calling.

corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is that public honor rightly follows, rather than substitutes for, private faithfulness already proven in character.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has simply become rare in ordinary speech rather than contested.

The pattern it names is worth recovering: Boaz's honor at the gate was conferred because his prior kindness to Ruth and Naomi had already shown him worthy of it, not the reverse. A culture that confers public honor first and hopes character will follow has inverted the order Ruth 4 actually commends.
roots_summary: From Old English weorthig, worthy, worthily names conduct that fits and earns given honor; Ruth 4:11 blesses Boaz to do worthily in Ephratah after his redemptive kindness.
